storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — radar is clear, skies are mostly clear, and it will simply be a cold, dry, breezy night with temperatures falling through the 40s.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer tonight: the Sound (54°F) is already 8°F warmer than the air at 4 PM and the gap widens to about 17°F by 8 PM as the air cools — the cove behaves like everywhere else.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: quiet. The New York radar shows no echoes anywhere in range, there are no National Weather Service alerts, and the atmosphere has no thunderstorm fuel at all (instability is zero, and the winds aloft are weak at about 9 kt of shear). Pressure is high and steady near 1020 hPa in a dry northwest flow behind the last system.

Local effect: none in play. The cove's usual protection comes from cool Sound water sitting under warmer air, which forms a stable layer that starves incoming storms. In mid-November it runs the other way: the water is 54°F while the air is about 46°F inland, so the air is already 8°F colder than the water at 4 PM.

How that evolves: the Sound holds its temperature while the air cools quickly after the 4:35 PM sunset, so the gap only moves further from the protective side — roughly 12°F colder than the water at 5 PM, 14°F at 6 PM and about 17°F by 8 PM. There is no point this evening when a marine layer exists, and no sea breeze either: every coastal station is blowing offshore from the northwest.

Most likely outcome: a dry evening for the cove and for the surrounding towns alike, with no difference between the shoreline and inland. Temperatures fall from about 50°F now to the upper 30s by 8 PM.

What would change the call: nothing visible in the next several hours. With no cells on radar there is nothing to time, so no arrival estimate is given.

wind.regime_label: Moderate northwest gradient wind — no sea breeze in play

hourly.shift_note: gusty off the land, easing after sunset
steady NW, gusts damping after dark

wind.tactics_blurb: Northwest wind blowing off the land: puffy and shifty, with the best average pressure in the middle of the cove away from the lee of the shoreline. Stay center, tack on the headers, and expect the breeze to ease from about 10 kt now to 6–8 kt after dark without dying.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The call: a moderate gradient wind from the northwest — the wind is driven by the large-scale pressure pattern, not by a sea breeze. The well-sited airport anemometers around the Sound average 10 kt, and Riverside YC in the cove is reading NW 11 kt gusting 18 (10-minute average 10 kt) at 4 PM. There is no thermal ingredient at all: the inland air is about 8°F colder than the Sound, and not one of 18 coastal stations has an onshore wind.

Will it hold: yes. A gradient wind does not depend on the sun, so the 4:35 PM sunset does not switch it off the way it kills a summer sea breeze. It does soften: as the land cools after dark the gusts lose their punch, and the average drifts from about 10 kt now to 7–9 kt through 6 PM and 6–7 kt later in the evening. The direction swings slightly right to north-northwest around 6 PM, then backs slowly left to about 310° by 8 PM.

Where the pressure sits: a northwest wind reaches the cove after crossing land, trees and houses, so it arrives in puffs with holes between them. The steadiest average breeze is usually mid-cove, clear of the immediate lee of the northwest shore. Expect swings of 15–30° with the puffs; these are oscillations rather than a one-way shift, so playing each header pays more than committing to a side.

Model vs. observations: the high-resolution forecast model is running behind the real wind on both counts. For 4 PM it called 301° at 6 kt, while the western-Sound stations sit at about 324° and the cove is at 10 kt. The speeds in the table are lifted a few knots above the raw model to match the cove, and the gap narrows after dark as the gusts damp. Because this is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day, the sea-breeze direction correction does not apply. The station network also shows only fair agreement on direction (73% within 45° of the median), which is typical of a gusty offshore flow in sheltered suburban sites rather than a sign of a front.

What it feels like: 6–10 kt is the sweet spot for dinghies, with gusts in the low-to-mid teens early in the window keeping it lively. It is dark for the whole window and cold — about 44°F at 5 PM falling to the upper 30s by 8 PM, over 54°F water.
